body: A compound biosynthesized by a bacterium that destroys or inhibits the growth of other microbes is a/an…

options.hint: Correct. Antibiotics are natural products of microbes that act against other microbes.
Synthetic drugs are made chemically, not by microbes.
A general term for any antimicrobial agent, natural or synthetic.
Describes a mechanism (e.g. sulfonamides), not a microbial product.

hint: Natural product of one microbe against another.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Strictly, an **antibiotic** is a substance produced by a microorganism (e.g. *Streptomyces*, *Penicillium*, *Bacillus*) that inhibits or kills other microorganisms. Synthetic agents (sulfonamides, quinolones) are chemotherapeutic drugs.

## Simplified explanation

An antibiotic is a **microbe-made** chemical that kills or stops other microbes.

body: Characteristics of a bacterial colony formed on culture plates include all the following EXCEPT…

options.hint: Colony size is a colonial feature.
Colony shape (form) is a colonial feature.
Pigment is a colonial feature.
Correct. Cell arrangement (chains, clusters) is seen microscopically, not as a colony feature.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Colonial morphology includes **size, shape/form, elevation, margin, colour, surface, opacity, consistency, odour and haemolysis**. Cell **arrangement** (pairs, chains, clusters) is a microscopic feature seen on a stained smear.

## Simplified explanation

Arrangement of cells is seen under the **microscope**, not by looking at a colony.

body: The MAIN host defence against bacterial exotoxins is:

options.text: Modulation of host cell receptors in response to the toxin
options.hint: Not a significant defence mechanism.
Macrophages do not neutralise circulating toxin.
Correct. Antitoxin antibodies bind and neutralise exotoxins.
They assist antibody production but do not neutralise toxin directly.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Exotoxins are proteins, so **neutralizing antibodies (antitoxins)**, mainly IgG with IgM early, bind them and block attachment to host cell receptors. This is the basis of toxoid vaccines (tetanus, diphtheria) and of antitoxin therapy.

## Simplified explanation

**Antibodies** neutralise bacterial toxins.

body: An elderly man with an enlarged prostate has frequent and painful urination. Suddenly he develops fever and chills. Examination reveals hypotension (blood pressure 55/10 mm Hg) and a blood culture is positive for *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. The fever, chills and hypotension likely derive from the bacterial…

options.hint: The capsule is antiphagocytic but does not produce these systemic effects.
Correct. The outer membrane carries LPS (endotoxin), the cause of Gram-negative sepsis.
Alpha toxin is a staphylococcal/clostridial exotoxin, not a Klebsiella product.
The capsule is antiphagocytic but does not produce these systemic effects.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Gram-negative sepsis is driven by **lipid A of LPS** in the **outer membrane**. Lipid A is recognised by TLR4 on macrophages, which release TNF-α, IL-1 and IL-6, producing fever, vasodilation and hypotension.

## Simplified explanation

Fever and shock come from **endotoxin (LPS)** in the Gram-negative **outer membrane**.

body: The MIC is the ………… of a drug that is required to inhibit growth of a microbe.

options.hint: Correct. MIC = minimum inhibitory concentration.
It is the minimum, not the maximum.
The MIC corresponds to the highest dilution that still inhibits growth.
Dose is a clinical term, not an in-vitro measurement.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**MIC (minimum inhibitory concentration)** is the lowest concentration of an antimicrobial that prevents visible growth after overnight incubation. The **MBC** is the lowest concentration that kills at least 99.9% of the inoculum.

## Simplified explanation

MIC = the **lowest amount** of drug that stops growth.

body: Virulence factors include all the following EXCEPT…

options.hint: Toxins are classic virulence factors.
Correct. The cell wall as a general structure is present in harmless bacteria too.
Capsules are antiphagocytic virulence factors.
Exoenzymes such as coagulase and hyaluronidase are virulence factors.

hint: Which is a basic structure of nearly all bacteria?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Virulence factors** are structures or products that increase the ability to cause disease: adhesins, capsules, toxins and invasive enzymes (coagulase, collagenase, hyaluronidase, IgA protease), plus siderophores. The cell wall is a universal structural component.

## Simplified explanation

Toxins, capsules and enzymes help bacteria cause disease; the ordinary **cell wall** is in all bacteria.

body: A positive antibody test for HIV would be a ………… of an infection.

options.hint: Correct. An objective, measurable finding is a sign.
A sequela is an after-effect of a disease.
Symptoms are subjective changes felt by the patient.
A syndrome is a characteristic group of signs and symptoms.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Signs** are objective changes that can be observed or measured (fever, rash, a laboratory result). **Symptoms** are subjective changes reported by the patient (pain, malaise). A **syndrome** is a cluster of both that characterises a disease.

## Simplified explanation

A result you can measure in the laboratory is a **sign**.

body: Which of the following is NOT a condition of Koch's postulates?

options.text: cultivate the microbe in a lab
options.hint: Isolation in pure culture is one of the postulates.

options.text: isolate the causative agent of a disease
options.hint: Finding and isolating the agent is one of the postulates.

options.text: test the effects of a pathogen on humans
options.hint: Correct. Koch used susceptible experimental animals, not humans.

options.text: inoculate a test animal to observe the disease
options.hint: Inoculation of a susceptible animal is one of the postulates.

hint: Think about what was ethically possible.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Koch's postulates: (1) the organism is found in every case of the disease; (2) it is isolated and grown in **pure culture**; (3) inoculation into a **susceptible animal** reproduces the disease; (4) the same organism is re-isolated from that animal.

## Simplified explanation

Koch tested germs in **animals**, not in people.

body: Which subset of white blood cells accounts for acquired, specific immunity?

options.hint: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes.
Correct. Lymphocytes (B and T cells) mediate specific immunity.
Monocytes belong to innate immunity and antigen presentation.
Macrophages belong to innate immunity and antigen presentation.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Adaptive (acquired) immunity** is antigen-specific and has memory; it is mediated by **lymphocytes** — B cells producing antibody and T cells providing cell-mediated immunity. Neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages belong to innate immunity.

## Simplified explanation

Specific immunity is the job of **lymphocytes** such as B cells.

body: The following statements concerning the mechanism of action of antimicrobial drugs are correct EXCEPT…

options.text: vancomycin acts by inhibiting peptidoglycan synthesis.
options.hint: True — it binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus.

options.text: erythromycin is a bactericidal drug that disrupts cell membranes.
options.hint: Correct. This is false — erythromycin is a bacteriostatic macrolide acting on the 50S ribosomal subunit.

options.text: quinolones, such as ciprofloxacin, act by inhibiting the DNA gyrase of bacteria.
options.hint: True.

options.text: aminoglycosides such as streptomycin are bactericidal drugs that inhibit protein synthesis.
options.hint: True — they bind the 30S subunit.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Erythromycin** binds the **50S** ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation; it is usually **bacteriostatic**. Membrane-active agents are the polymyxins and daptomycin, not macrolides.

## Simplified explanation

Erythromycin **stops protein synthesis**; it does not act on the membrane.

body: Which one of the following best describes the mechanism by which immunopathogenesis occurs? The ability of…

options.text: cytotoxic T cells to cause pathogenesis by viruses
options.hint: Correct. Immunopathogenesis is tissue damage caused by the host's own immune response.

options.text: cytotoxic T cells to block pathogenesis by viruses
options.hint: That is protective immunity, not immunopathogenesis.

options.text: neutrophils to block pathogenesis by viruses
options.hint: That is protective immunity.

options.text: antibodies to block pathogenesis by viruses
options.hint: That is protective immunity.

hint: Damage caused by the immune response itself.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Immunopathogenesis** means the signs of disease are produced by the immune response rather than by the microbe directly — for example cytotoxic T cells destroying infected hepatocytes in hepatitis B, immune-complex deposition, or excessive cytokine release.

## Simplified explanation

Sometimes the **immune system itself** causes the damage, as when killer T cells destroy infected cells.

body: Which of the following organisms is most likely to be implicated in dental caries?

options.hint: A skin commensal.
Not a cause of caries.
Correct. It forms dextran plaque and produces lactic acid.
A colonic organism.

hint: A viridans streptococcus of the mouth.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*Streptococcus mutans* converts sucrose into **dextran (glucan)**, which forms dental plaque, and ferments sugars to **lactic acid**, which demineralises enamel.

## Simplified explanation

*S. mutans* makes sticky plaque and acid that damages teeth.

body: Infection by which one of the following bacteria is most likely to be interrupted by handwashing?

options.hint: Transmitted mainly from maternal genital flora at birth.
Correct. Spread largely by hands and contact, so hand hygiene interrupts it.
Transmitted sexually and transplacentally.
Transmitted by tick bite.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

*S. aureus* is carried on skin and in the anterior nares and is transferred by **hands** — the main route of cross-infection in hospitals. **Hand hygiene** is therefore the single most effective control measure. The others spread sexually, vertically or by arthropod vectors.

## Simplified explanation

*S. aureus* travels on **hands**, so washing hands stops it.

body: Drugs that prevent the formation of the bacterial cell wall are…

options.hint: Quinolones inhibit DNA gyrase.
Tetracyclines inhibit the 30S ribosomal subunit.
Correct. Penicillins and cephalosporins block peptidoglycan cross-linking.
Aminoglycosides inhibit protein synthesis at the 30S subunit.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**β-lactams** (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams) bind penicillin-binding proteins and inhibit the **transpeptidation** step of peptidoglycan cross-linking, so the wall weakens and the cell lyses. Vancomycin and bacitracin also act on wall synthesis by other steps.

## Simplified explanation

**β-lactams** such as penicillin stop bacteria building their cell wall.

body: A teenage boy has developed a tender, painful lump in his axilla. The lesion eventually came to a "point" and drained purulent material. A Gram stain of the pus revealed WBCs and Gram-positive cocci. Which of the following would be the most probable source of this infection?

options.hint: Food-borne staphylococcal illness causes vomiting, not abscesses.
Not the usual source of a staphylococcal abscess.
Pool water is associated with Pseudomonas folliculitis, not this picture.
Correct. The boy's own skin/nasal S. aureus is the usual source of a boil.

hint: Where does S. aureus normally live?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A boil (furuncle) is typically caused by **S. aureus** from the patient's own **resident flora** (anterior nares, skin), which enters through a hair follicle. Gram-positive cocci in clusters within pus support this.

## Simplified explanation

The germ comes from the patient's **own skin and nose bacteria**.

body: Microbial resistance to drugs is acquired through all the following EXCEPT…

options.hint: Correct. 'Transfer' alone is not one of the defined mechanisms of gene exchange.
Conjugation transfers R plasmids.
Phage-mediated transfer of resistance genes occurs.
Uptake of free DNA can transfer resistance genes.

hint: Name the three classical modes of gene exchange.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Acquired resistance arises by **mutation** or by horizontal gene transfer through the three classical mechanisms: **conjugation, transduction and transformation** (plus transposition of mobile elements). 'Transfer' is a generic word, not a specific mechanism.

## Simplified explanation

The named ways are **conjugation, transduction and transformation**.

body: The specific action of haemolysins is to…

options.hint: That is the action of leukocidins.
Correct. Haemolysins lyse erythrocytes.
An inflammatory response, not a toxin action.
Pyrogens such as endotoxin cause fever.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Haemolysins** are exotoxins that lyse **red blood cells**, releasing haemoglobin and iron for bacterial use. On blood agar they produce α (partial, green), β (complete, clear) or γ (none) haemolysis — an important identification feature.

## Simplified explanation

Haemolysins **break open red blood cells**.

body: A short period early in a disease that manifests with general malaise and achiness is the…

options.hint: A sequela follows after the illness.
Correct. The prodromal period has vague, general symptoms.
The invasion/illness period has the characteristic signs.
Incubation is before any symptoms appear.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Disease stages: **incubation** (no symptoms) → **prodromal** (short, vague, general symptoms such as malaise and aching) → **period of invasion/illness** (characteristic signs, peak severity) → **decline** → **convalescence**.

## Simplified explanation

The vague "coming down with something" stage is the **prodrome**.

body: Which non-specific host defence is associated with the trachea?

options.hint: Lactic acid is a vaginal and skin defence.
Tears protect the eye.
Correct. The mucociliary escalator of the trachea removes trapped microbes.
Shedding is a skin defence.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The tracheobronchial tree is lined by **ciliated columnar epithelium with mucus**. Trapped particles and microbes are swept upward to the pharynx and swallowed or coughed out. Smoking and some toxins (pertussis) impair ciliary action.

## Simplified explanation

Tiny hairs (**cilia**) in the windpipe sweep germs out.

body: The term vertical transmission refers to transmission…

options.hint: Correct. Vertical transmission is from parent to offspring.

options.text: from a sex worker to a client.
options.hint: That is horizontal (direct contact) transmission.

options.text: from one child to another at school.
options.hint: That is horizontal transmission.

options.text: by insect vector from reservoir to patient.
options.hint: That is vector-borne horizontal transmission.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Vertical transmission** passes an agent from **mother to offspring** — transplacentally (rubella, *T. pallidum*, HIV, CMV, toxoplasma), during delivery (HBV, HSV, gonococcus, GBS) or by breast milk. Everything else is horizontal.

## Simplified explanation

Vertical = **mother to baby**.

body: An example of a non-specific chemical barrier to infection is…

options.hint: A physical/mechanical barrier.
A mechanical barrier.
Correct. Bile is a chemical antimicrobial barrier.

options.text: sloughing of epithelium as it grows
options.hint: A mechanical barrier.

hint: Which one works by chemistry, not by physical removal?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Chemical barriers** of innate immunity include gastric acid, **bile salts**, lysozyme in tears and saliva, fatty acids and low pH of skin, lactic acid in the vagina, and antimicrobial peptides (defensins). Skin, cilia and desquamation are **physical/mechanical** barriers.

## Simplified explanation

**Bile** kills microbes chemically; the others work by physically blocking or sweeping them away.

body: Which of the following is an enterotoxin?

options.hint: The plague (murine) toxin is not an enterotoxin.
Correct. Cholera toxin acts on the small intestine to cause watery diarrhoea.
Diphtheria toxin is a cytotoxin that blocks protein synthesis.
LPS is endotoxin, not an enterotoxin.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Enterotoxins** act on the intestinal mucosa to cause diarrhoea or vomiting. **Cholera toxin** (A-B toxin) ADP-ribosylates Gs, raising cAMP and causing massive secretion of chloride and water. Other enterotoxins: staphylococcal enterotoxins, ETEC LT and ST, *C. perfringens* enterotoxin.

## Simplified explanation

**Cholera toxin** acts on the gut, so it is an enterotoxin.

body: Molecular methods employed in the diagnosis of bacteria include all the following EXCEPT…

options.hint: Correct. This is a serological (antibody-based) method, not a molecular one.
A genotypic method based on DNA base composition.
DNA probe hybridization is a molecular method.
Nucleic acid sequencing is a molecular method.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Molecular (genotypic)** methods examine nucleic acids: %G+C, DNA–DNA hybridization, probes, PCR, 16S rRNA sequencing, RFLP/PFGE. **Complement fixation** is a classical **serological** assay that detects antigen–antibody reactions.

## Simplified explanation

Complement fixation is an **antibody test**, not a DNA test.

body: Each of the following statements regarding the selective action of antibiotics on bacteria is correct EXCEPT…

options.text: Chloramphenicol affects the large subunit of the bacterial ribosome, which is different from the large subunit of the human ribosome.
options.hint: True — bacterial 50S versus human 60S.

options.text: Isoniazid affects the DNA polymerase of bacteria but not that of human cells.
options.hint: Correct. This is false — isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall.

options.text: Sulfonamides affect folic acid synthesis in bacteria, a pathway that does not occur in human cells.
options.hint: True — humans take up preformed folate.

options.text: Penicillins affect bacteria rather than human cells because bacteria have a cell wall, whereas human cells do not.
options.hint: True.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Isoniazid** is a prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG); it inhibits **InhA**, blocking **mycolic acid** synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall. Rifampicin, not isoniazid, acts on a polymerase (bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase).

## Simplified explanation

Isoniazid blocks the **waxy wall** of mycobacteria, not DNA polymerase.

body: Which one of the following BEST describes the mode of action of endotoxin?

options.text: Causes the release of tumor necrosis factor
options.hint: Correct. LPS triggers macrophages to release TNF-α and other cytokines.
That is the action of lecithinase (C. perfringens alpha toxin).
That is diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.
That is botulinum toxin.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Endotoxin (**lipid A of LPS**) binds LBP/CD14/**TLR4** on macrophages, which release **TNF-α, IL-1 and IL-6**. These mediate fever, hypotension, neutrophil activation and, at high levels, disseminated intravascular coagulation.

## Simplified explanation

Endotoxin makes the body release **cytokines such as TNF**, which cause fever and shock.

body: The time that lapses between an encounter with a pathogen and the first symptom is…

options.hint: The prodrome is the first, vague symptoms themselves.
The invasion period is when characteristic signs appear.
Correct. Incubation is from exposure to the first symptom.
Convalescence is recovery after the illness.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **incubation period** runs from infection to the appearance of the first symptoms; its length depends on the organism's generation time, dose, route and host resistance (hours for staphylococcal food poisoning, years for leprosy or HIV).

## Simplified explanation

The quiet time between catching the germ and feeling ill is the **incubation period**.

body: Accessibility of a virus to host tissue is influenced by all the following EXCEPT…

options.hint: Skin and mucosal barriers affect access.
Innate defences affect access.

options.text: Distance to be traversed within the body
options.hint: Distance to the target organ affects access.

options.text: The intracellular environment that permits virus replication
options.hint: Correct. This determines replication once inside, not access to the tissue.

hint: Which factor acts only after entry?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Access (tropism at the tissue level) depends on **barriers, innate defences and the distance/route** the virus must travel. Whether the cell's **intracellular environment** supports replication determines **permissiveness**, a separate step that follows successful access and receptor binding.

## Simplified explanation

The inside of the cell matters **after** the virus arrives, not for getting there.

body: An infection acquired during a stay or visit to a hospital is called…

options.hint: A focal infection spreads from a local site to other sites.
A zoonosis is acquired from animals.
Subclinical means without obvious symptoms.
Correct. Nosocomial (healthcare-associated) infections are acquired in hospital.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Nosocomial** infections are neither present nor incubating on admission, appearing usually after 48 hours. Common examples: catheter-associated UTI, ventilator-associated pneumonia, surgical site infection and intravascular device bacteraemia; frequent agents include *E. coli*, *S. aureus*, *P. aeruginosa* and *C. difficile*.

## Simplified explanation

An infection caught **in hospital** is nosocomial.

body: Which of the following blood cells function primarily as phagocytes?

options.hint: Basophils release histamine; they are not major phagocytes.
Eosinophils mainly act against helminths and in allergy.
Correct. Neutrophils are the principal circulating phagocytes.
Lymphocytes mediate specific immunity and do not phagocytose.

hint: The most numerous white cell in acute infection.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Neutrophils (polymorphs)** are the first and most numerous phagocytes recruited to bacterial infection; monocytes/macrophages are the other main phagocytes. Basophils and eosinophils have mainly inflammatory and antiparasitic roles.

## Simplified explanation

**Neutrophils** are the main 'eating' white cells.

body: Which of the following is the end product of the complement system?

options.hint: Properdin stabilises the alternative pathway C3 convertase.
That describes the process, not the product.
C9 is a component of the final complex, not the end product itself.
Correct. C5b6789 forms the MAC, the terminal product.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

All three complement pathways converge on C3 and C5 cleavage, ending in the **membrane attack complex (C5b, C6, C7, C8 and multiple C9)**, which creates pores and lyses susceptible cells (notably *Neisseria*). Other products include opsonin C3b and anaphylatoxins C3a/C5a.

## Simplified explanation

Complement finishes by building the **membrane attack complex** that punches holes in cells.

body: The MOST important function of antibody in host defences against bacteria is…

options.hint: Correct. Opsonisation by IgG greatly enhances phagocytosis.
Antibody neutralises rather than digests toxins.
Antibodies do not enter bacteria.

options.text: activation of lysozyme that degrades the cell wall
options.hint: Lysozyme acts independently of antibody.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

IgG bound to a bacterial surface is recognised by **Fcγ receptors** on neutrophils and macrophages, and complement activation deposits **C3b**; both act as **opsonins**, dramatically increasing phagocytosis. Antibody also neutralises toxins and adhesins and activates complement.

## Simplified explanation

Antibodies **coat bacteria** so white cells can eat them easily.

body: Each of the following statements concerning penicillin is correct EXCEPT…

options.text: an intact β-lactam ring of penicillin is required for its activity.
options.hint: True — β-lactamase opens the ring and abolishes activity.

options.text: the structure of penicillin resembles that of a dipeptide of alanine.
options.hint: True — it mimics D-alanyl-D-alanine.

options.text: penicillin is a bacteriostatic drug because autolytic enzymes are *not* activated.
options.hint: Correct. This is false — penicillin is bactericidal and does activate autolysins.

options.text: penicillin inhibits transpeptidases, which are required for cross-linking peptidoglycan.
options.hint: True.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Penicillin binds PBPs (transpeptidases), halting cross-linking, and also **activates autolysins**, so growing cells lyse. It is therefore **bactericidal** against dividing organisms. Tolerance occurs in strains with deficient autolysin activity.

## Simplified explanation

Penicillin **kills** growing bacteria; it is not bacteriostatic.

body: Which of the following is associated with bacterial invasion?

options.hint: An enzyme that damages membranes but is classed as a toxin.
Correct. Collagenase breaks down connective tissue and spreads infection.
A toxin that lyses red cells.
A host antimicrobial peptide, not a bacterial product.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Invasins/spreading factors** break down host tissue barriers: **collagenase** (*C. perfringens*), **hyaluronidase** and **streptokinase** (*S. pyogenes*), and coagulase/staphylokinase. Defensins are host-derived antimicrobial peptides.

## Simplified explanation

**Collagenase** digests tissue so bacteria can spread.

body: An antibiotic that disrupts the normal flora can cause…

options.hint: Tooth staining is a specific side effect of tetracyclines in children, not a flora effect.
Correct. Loss of colonization resistance allows overgrowth of resistant organisms.
A direct toxic effect of chloramphenicol, not a flora effect.
A direct drug toxicity, not a flora effect.

hint: Overgrowth after the flora is removed.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Broad-spectrum antibiotics suppress the normal flora, removing **colonization resistance**; resistant organisms overgrow — *Clostridioides difficile* (antibiotic-associated colitis), *Candida* (thrush, vaginitis), resistant Gram-negative rods. This is a **superinfection**.

## Simplified explanation

Killing the good bacteria lets other germs take over — a **superinfection**.

body: Opsonization is the process by which…

options.text: chemokines attract neutrophils to the site of infection.
options.hint: That is chemotaxis.

options.text: the alternate pathway of complement is activated.
options.hint: Complement activation is separate, though it produces opsonins.

options.text: bacteria are made more easily phagocytized.
options.hint: Correct. Opsonins coat microbes to promote their ingestion.
That is a systemic inflammatory response.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Opsonins** — IgG (via Fcγ receptors), **C3b** (via CR1) and mannose-binding lectin or CRP — coat microbes so phagocytes bind and ingest them far more efficiently. Encapsulated bacteria resist phagocytosis until opsonised.

## Simplified explanation

Opsonisation **coats germs** so white cells can swallow them.

body: Each of the following statements concerning the mechanism of action of antibacterial drugs is correct EXCEPT:

options.text: Cephalosporins are bactericidal drugs that inhibit the transpeptidase reaction and prevent cell wall synthesis.
options.hint: True.

options.text: Tetracyclines are bacteriostatic drugs that inhibit protein synthesis by blocking tRNA binding.
options.hint: True — they block the 30S A site.

options.text: Aminoglycosides are bacteriostatic drugs that inhibit protein synthesis by activating ribonuclease, which degrades mRNA.
options.hint: Correct. This is false — aminoglycosides are bactericidal and act by binding the 30S subunit, causing misreading.

options.text: Erythromycin is a bacteriostatic drug that inhibits protein synthesis by blocking translocation of the polypeptide.
options.hint: True.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Aminoglycosides** (gentamicin, streptomycin) bind irreversibly to the **30S** subunit, causing **misreading of mRNA** and blocking initiation; they are **bactericidal** and concentration-dependent. They do not activate ribonuclease.

## Simplified explanation

Aminoglycosides **kill** bacteria by making them misread their mRNA.

body: Which statement is NOT an aim in the use of drugs in antimicrobial chemotherapy? The drug should be…

options.hint: Killing the organism is a desirable aim.
Selective toxicity is the central principle.
Activity at low concentrations is desirable.
Correct. Rapid breakdown and excretion would shorten the drug's useful action.

hint: Which property would work against treatment?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

An ideal antimicrobial is **selectively toxic**, **microbicidal**, active at low concentrations, stable, non-allergenic, well distributed to the site of infection and **not** removed from the body so rapidly that effective levels cannot be maintained.

## Simplified explanation

A drug that is destroyed and passed out **too quickly** would not stay long enough to work.

body: An unusual response to a drug or any external agent is…

options.hint: Resistance is a property of the microbe, not a host response.
Superinfection is overgrowth of other organisms.
Toxicity is a dose-related, predictable effect.
Correct. An allergy is an unusual, immunologically mediated response.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Allergy (hypersensitivity)** is an unpredictable, immune-mediated reaction occurring in sensitised individuals, e.g. penicillin rash or anaphylaxis. **Toxicity** is dose-related and occurs in everyone at high enough exposure.

## Simplified explanation

An unexpected, **immune** reaction to a drug is an allergy.

body: Which of the following modes of action would be most selectively toxic?

options.hint: Human ribosomes differ but are still ribosomes, so less selective.
Correct. Human cells have no cell wall at all.
Human membranes are similar to bacterial membranes.
Human cells also replicate DNA.

hint: Which structure is absent from human cells?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Selective toxicity** is greatest when the target is absent from host cells. Human cells have **no peptidoglycan cell wall**, so β-lactams and vancomycin are very safe. Membrane-active agents are the least selective because membranes are chemically similar.

## Simplified explanation

People have no **cell wall**, so wall-blocking drugs are safest.

body: An example of a non-communicable infection is…

options.hint: Spread person to person by droplet nuclei.
Highly communicable.
Communicable with prolonged close contact.
Correct. Tetanus is acquired from spores in soil, not from other people.

hint: Which one is not passed from person to person?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **non-communicable** infection is not transmitted from host to host. *Clostridium tetani* spores enter through wounds from **soil and dust**; the patient is not infectious to others. Tuberculosis, measles and leprosy all spread between people.

## Simplified explanation

**Tetanus** comes from soil, not from another person.

body: Which of the following would NOT be a portal of entry?

options.hint: The skin (through cuts, bites and follicles) is a portal of entry.
Correct. The meninges are an internal site reached after entry, not a portal.
The placenta is the portal for vertical transmission.
Part of the gastrointestinal portal.

hint: Portals are surfaces open to the outside.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Portals of entry** are the mucous membranes (respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, conjunctiva), the **skin**, the **parenteral route** and the **placenta**. The **meninges** are an internal structure, infected after the organism has already entered and spread.

## Simplified explanation

The meninges are **inside** the body, so they are not a way in.

body: Immunologic memory refers to the ability of the immune system to…

options.hint: Correct. Memory cells give a faster, stronger secondary response.
That is diversity, not memory.

options.text: react with millions of different antigens
options.hint: That is diversity/specificity.

options.text: migrate from the blood vessels into the tissues
options.hint: That is diapedesis.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Memory** B and T cells persist after an infection or vaccination. On re-exposure they produce a **secondary (anamnestic) response**: shorter lag, higher titre, mainly IgG, and higher affinity — the basis of long-lasting vaccine protection and booster doses.

## Simplified explanation

The immune system **remembers** a germ and responds faster next time.

body: Each of the following statements about the resistance of bacteria to antimicrobial drugs is correct EXCEPT…

options.text: resistance to tetracycline is known to be due to an enzyme that hydrolyzes the ester linkage
options.hint: Correct. This is false — tetracycline resistance is mainly due to efflux pumps and ribosomal protection, not an ester-hydrolysing enzyme.

options.text: resistance to chloramphenicol is known to be due to an enzyme that acetylates the drug
options.hint: True — chloramphenicol acetyltransferase.

options.text: resistance to penicillin is known to be due to reduced affinity of transpeptidases
options.hint: True — altered PBPs, as in MRSA and pneumococci.

options.text: resistance to penicillin is known to be due to cleavage by β-lactamase
options.hint: True.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Tetracycline resistance is usually by **active efflux (tet pumps)** or **ribosomal protection proteins (TetM/TetO)**, sometimes enzymatic inactivation by TetX (an oxidoreductase, not an esterase). Chloramphenicol is inactivated by **acetyltransferase**; penicillin resistance arises from **β-lactamases** or **altered PBPs**.

## Simplified explanation

Bacteria resist tetracycline mainly by **pumping it out** or protecting their ribosome.

body: Organisms that produce endotoxin include all the following EXCEPT…

options.hint: A Gram-negative rod, so it has LPS.
A Gram-negative rod, so it has LPS.
Correct. It is Gram-positive, so it has no lipopolysaccharide.
A Gram-negative coccus with lipooligosaccharide.

hint: Endotoxin belongs to one Gram group.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Endotoxin is lipopolysaccharide of the Gram-negative outer membrane**. Gram-positive organisms such as *Clostridium*, *Staphylococcus* and *Streptococcus* have no LPS; their cell wall components (lipoteichoic acid, peptidoglycan) can produce similar inflammation but are not endotoxin.

## Simplified explanation

Only **Gram-negative** bacteria have endotoxin; *C. tetani* is Gram-positive.

body: True or false: antigenic variation allows pathogens to stay ahead of the immune response of the host.

options.hint: Correct. Changing surface antigens lets the organism escape existing antibodies.
Antigenic variation does help pathogens evade immunity.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Antigenic variation** changes surface antigens so that antibodies raised against earlier variants no longer bind: influenza antigenic drift and shift, *Borrelia* relapsing fever, *N. gonorrhoeae* pilin variation, trypanosome VSG switching. It is a major obstacle to vaccine development.

## Simplified explanation

If the germ keeps **changing its coat**, old antibodies no longer recognise it.

body: True or false: for most viruses the portal of entry is the same as the portal of exit.

options.hint: Correct. Most viruses leave by the route through which they entered.
For most viruses entry and exit routes do coincide.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Respiratory viruses enter and leave in respiratory secretions; enteric viruses enter and leave by the faecal–oral route. Exceptions exist (e.g. arboviruses enter by bite and leave in blood taken by a vector; rabies enters by bite and exits in saliva).

## Simplified explanation

Most viruses leave **the same way they came in**.

body: True or false: most bacteria that produce exotoxins are Gram-positive.

options.hint: Correct. Exotoxin production is characteristic of many Gram-positive pathogens.
Classically, exotoxins are associated mainly with Gram-positive organisms.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Classical teaching: **exotoxins** are secreted proteins produced mainly by **Gram-positive** organisms (*Clostridium*, *Corynebacterium*, *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*), although several Gram-negatives also produce them (*V. cholerae*, ETEC, *P. aeruginosa*). **Endotoxin** is confined to Gram-negatives.

## Simplified explanation

Mostly **Gram-positive** bacteria make exotoxins.

body: True or false: the volume of specimen to be collected for microbial diagnosis depends on age.

options.hint: Correct. Paediatric specimens, especially blood cultures, are smaller volumes.
Volume does vary with the patient's age and size.

hint: Think of blood culture volumes in babies.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Specimen volume affects sensitivity (particularly for **blood cultures**), but the volume taken must be safe for the patient. Paediatric blood culture bottles take 1–3 mL, whereas 8–10 mL per adult bottle is recommended.

## Simplified explanation

You take **smaller samples from children** than from adults.

body: True or false: very few microbes are always pathogenic.

options.hint: Correct. Most microbes are harmless or opportunistic; only a minority are true pathogens.
Obligate pathogens are in fact a small minority of microbes.

hint: How many microbes actually cause disease?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The vast majority of microorganisms are **saprophytes or commensals**. A limited number are **true (primary) pathogens** causing disease in healthy hosts (*M. tuberculosis*, *S. typhi*, *N. gonorrhoeae*), while many others are **opportunists** acting only when host defences are impaired.

## Simplified explanation

Only a **small number** of microbes always cause disease.

body: True or false: vertical transmission of viral infection can be achieved through the bite of an infected animal.

options.hint: An animal bite is horizontal, not vertical, transmission.
Correct. Vertical transmission is from mother to offspring; an animal bite is horizontal transmission.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Vertical** transmission passes from **mother to offspring** (transplacental, perinatal, breast milk). The bite of an infected animal (e.g. rabies) is **horizontal zoonotic** transmission.

## Simplified explanation

A bite is **not** mother-to-baby spread, so the statement is false.

body: True or false: all humans serving as reservoirs of an infection are carriers.

options.hint: Some human reservoirs are frankly ill cases, not carriers.
Correct. Human reservoirs include symptomatic cases as well as asymptomatic carriers.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A **carrier** harbours and sheds an organism **without clinical disease** (incubatory, convalescent, chronic or healthy carrier). A human **reservoir** may equally be a person with active disease, so not every reservoir is a carrier.

## Simplified explanation

Reservoirs include **sick people too**, not only silent carriers.

body: True or false: urine samples are usually cultured on CLED agar.

options.hint: Correct. CLED is the standard urine culture medium.
CLED agar is indeed the routine medium for urine.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**CLED agar** supports both Gram-positive and Gram-negative urinary pathogens, differentiates lactose fermenters (yellow) from non-fermenters (blue), and is **electrolyte deficient** so that *Proteus* does not swarm. MacConkey or blood agar may be used alongside it.

## Simplified explanation

Urine is usually plated on **CLED agar**, which stops *Proteus* swarming.

body: True or false: signs are subjective changes in body function that can be measured.

options.hint: Signs are objective, not subjective.
Correct. Signs are objective; symptoms are the subjective changes.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Signs** are **objective** changes that can be observed or measured by another person (fever, rash, leucocytosis). **Symptoms** are **subjective** changes felt and reported by the patient (headache, nausea).

## Simplified explanation

Signs are what others can **see or measure**, so calling them subjective is wrong.

body: True or false: formation of viral inclusion bodies is of no diagnostic significance.

options.hint: Inclusion bodies are in fact diagnostically useful.
Correct. Inclusion bodies such as Negri bodies are diagnostically useful.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Viral **inclusion bodies** are characteristic accumulations in infected cells and help diagnosis: **Negri bodies** (rabies, cytoplasmic), **Cowdry type A** (herpes, intranuclear), owl's-eye inclusions (CMV), Guarnieri bodies (poxviruses).

## Simplified explanation

Inclusion bodies **do help** diagnose some viral infections.

body: True or false: *Neisseria meningitidis* is oxidase positive.

options.hint: Correct. All Neisseria species are oxidase positive.
Neisseria are oxidase positive.

hint: A key screening test for Neisseria.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Oxidase positivity** (cytochrome c oxidase) is a key screening test for *Neisseria*, *Moraxella*, *Pseudomonas*, *Vibrio*, *Campylobacter* and *Helicobacter*; Enterobacteriaceae are oxidase negative. *N. meningitidis* also ferments glucose and maltose.

## Simplified explanation

*Neisseria* species, including the meningococcus, are **oxidase positive**.

body: True or false: pathogenicity is the degree or intensity of virulence of an organism.

options.hint: The definition is the other way round.
Correct. Virulence is the degree of pathogenicity, not the reverse.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Pathogenicity** is the *ability* of an organism to cause disease. **Virulence** is the **degree or intensity** of that pathogenicity, measured by indicators such as ID₅₀ and LD₅₀.

## Simplified explanation

Virulence measures **how strongly** a pathogen causes disease, so the statement is reversed.

body: True or false: most viral infections are asymptomatic.

options.hint: Correct. Subclinical (inapparent) infections outnumber clinical cases for most viruses.
Asymptomatic infection is in fact the commoner outcome for most viruses.

hint: Think of polio and hepatitis A in children.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

For most viruses the **subclinical:clinical ratio** is high — for example about 99:1 for poliovirus. Asymptomatic infection still induces immunity and still allows transmission, which matters greatly for control.

## Simplified explanation

Most people infected by a virus **never feel ill**.

body:
Differentiate between the following:

1. Chronic and latent infections
2. Bacteraemia and septicaemia
3. Epidemic infection and endemic infection
answer:
1. **Chronic infection** — the organism is continuously present and detectable, and the illness develops slowly and persists for a long time (e.g. tuberculosis, hepatitis B). **Latent infection** — the organism persists in a **silent, non-replicating** form with no symptoms or shedding between episodes, and may **reactivate** later (e.g. herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, *M. tuberculosis* latency).
2. **Bacteraemia** — the mere **presence of bacteria in the blood**, often transient and without symptoms (e.g. after tooth brushing). **Septicaemia** — bacteria are **multiplying in the blood** and causing systemic illness with fever, rigors and, if severe, shock.
3. **Epidemic** — a disease occurring in **unusually large numbers** in a population in a short period, above the expected level. **Endemic** — a disease **constantly present** at a fairly steady, expected level in a given population or area.

> [!answer]
> Chronic = persistent active disease; latent = silent with possible reactivation. Bacteraemia = bacteria present in blood; septicaemia = bacteria multiplying and causing systemic illness. Epidemic = sudden excess of cases; endemic = constant background level.
hint: Persistent vs silent; present vs multiplying; excess vs usual level.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These distinctions matter clinically and epidemiologically. Latency is typical of herpesviruses and of untreated tuberculosis infection; blood cultures distinguish transient bacteraemia from true septicaemia; and the endemic baseline is what defines whether a rise amounts to an epidemic (a pandemic being an epidemic across countries or continents).

## Simplified explanation

Chronic = long and active; latent = hiding quietly. Bacteraemia = germs just in the blood; septicaemia = germs growing and making you ill. Epidemic = sudden rise; endemic = always around.

body: (a) What is **combination therapy**? (b) Give **two** reasons why it is used.
answer:
**(a)** Combination therapy is the simultaneous use of **two or more antimicrobial agents** to treat a single infection.

**(b)** Reasons (any two):

1. To **prevent or delay the emergence of resistance** (e.g. tuberculosis therapy).
2. To achieve a **synergistic** effect (e.g. penicillin plus an aminoglycoside for enterococcal endocarditis).
3. To provide **broad empirical cover** in serious infection before the organism is identified.
4. To treat **mixed (polymicrobial) infections**, such as intra-abdominal sepsis.
5. To allow **lower doses** of a toxic drug, reducing toxicity.

> [!answer]
> Using two or more antimicrobials together — to prevent resistance, obtain synergy, cover mixed infections, or give broad empirical cover.
hint: Think of how tuberculosis is treated.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Combination therapy also carries risks: antagonism (e.g. a bacteriostatic drug reducing the effect of a cell-wall-active bactericidal drug), added toxicity, cost and greater disturbance of the normal flora, so it should be rationalised once culture results are available.

## Simplified explanation

Using **more than one antibiotic together**, mainly to stop resistance developing and to cover more organisms.

body: State any **four** criteria for rejecting specimens for the diagnosis of infectious diseases.
answer:
Any four:

1. **Unlabelled or wrongly labelled** specimen, or details not matching the request form.
2. **Inappropriate or leaking container**, broken container, or specimen contaminated on the outside.
3. **Wrong transport medium, preservative or anticoagulant** for the test requested.
4. **Excessive delay** between collection and receipt, or incorrect storage temperature.
5. **Insufficient quantity** for the tests requested.
6. An **unsuitable specimen type** for the investigation (e.g. saliva instead of sputum; swab when tissue or fluid is required).
7. **Duplicate specimen** from the same site on the same day, or a specimen obviously contaminated with normal flora.
8. No request form, or no test specified.

> [!answer]
> Unlabelled/mislabelled, leaking or wrong container, wrong or missing transport medium, excessive delay or wrong storage, insufficient volume, or an inappropriate specimen type.
hint: Think of what makes a result unreliable.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Rejection criteria protect the patient from wrong results. The laboratory should record the rejection, notify the requester promptly and ask for a repeat, since a poor specimen yields a misleading answer that may be more harmful than no answer.

## Simplified explanation

Reject a sample if it is **badly labelled, badly collected, too old, too little, or the wrong type**.

body: Mention **four** biochemical or metabolic characteristics of microorganisms that can aid in the identification of microorganisms.
answer:
Any four:

1. **Catalase** production (staphylococci positive, streptococci negative).
2. **Oxidase** production (*Neisseria*, *Pseudomonas*, *Vibrio* positive; Enterobacteriaceae negative).
3. **Coagulase** production (*S. aureus* positive).
4. **Carbohydrate fermentation** patterns (e.g. lactose fermentation on MacConkey).
5. **Urease** production (*Proteus*, *H. pylori*).
6. **Indole** production from tryptophan (*E. coli* positive).
7. **H₂S** production on TSI/KIA (*Salmonella*, *Proteus*).
8. **Citrate** utilisation; **nitrate reduction**; **gelatin liquefaction**; **DNase**; **haemolysis** on blood agar.

> [!answer]
> e.g. catalase, oxidase, coagulase, urease, indole, H₂S production and sugar fermentation patterns.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These tests are combined into identification schemes and commercial galleries (API strips) or automated systems, and increasingly confirmed by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry or 16S rRNA sequencing.

## Simplified explanation

Tests such as **catalase, oxidase, coagulase, urease, indole and sugar fermentation** tell organisms apart.

body: Give **three** reasons why a virus can infect cells but not be able to replicate in them.
answer:
1. The cell is **non-permissive** — it lacks the transcription factors, enzymes or other host factors the virus needs, so replication is blocked after entry (abortive infection).
2. The virus has entered a **latent state**, with its genome maintained (episomally or integrated) and lytic genes repressed.
3. The virus is **defective** (lacks a functional gene) and needs a helper virus, e.g. hepatitis D requiring HBV.
4. **Host restriction factors or interferon-induced antiviral proteins** block replication.
5. The virus is **inactivated/degraded** intracellularly, e.g. in a lysosome, or the cell dies before progeny are made.

> [!answer]
> The cell is non-permissive, the virus becomes latent, the virus is defective and needs a helper, or host restriction/interferon responses block replication.
hint: Infection and replication are separate steps.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Susceptibility** (having the receptor) and **permissiveness** (supporting replication) are distinct. A cell may be susceptible but non-permissive, giving an **abortive** infection; a permissive cell without receptors can still be infected by transfected nucleic acid.

## Simplified explanation

Getting in is not enough — the cell must also have **what the virus needs to copy itself**, and the virus must not be defective or switched off.

body: Mention the **three** physical forms of culture media.
answer:
1. **Liquid (broth)** media
2. **Semi-solid** media
3. **Solid (agar)** media

> [!answer]
> Liquid (broth), semi-solid and solid media.
hint: Based on how much agar is present.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Agar content determines the form: **none** for broths (used for enrichment and blood cultures), about **0.2–0.5%** for semi-solid media (motility and transport media such as Cary–Blair), and **1.5–2%** for solid media (plates and slopes, used for isolating colonies).

## Simplified explanation

Media come as **liquid, semi-solid and solid**.

body: What is the sterilizing agent used in autoclaves?
answer:
**Saturated steam under pressure** (moist heat) — typically at 121°C and 15 psi for 15 minutes.

> [!answer]
> Saturated steam under pressure (moist heat).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

It is the **steam**, not the pressure, that sterilizes: steam condensing on a cooler surface releases its latent heat and wets the item, coagulating microbial proteins. Air must be displaced, since trapped air lowers the temperature reached at a given pressure.

## Simplified explanation

The autoclave sterilizes with **steam under pressure**.

body: What is the main purpose of **inverting culture plates** during incubation?
answer:
To prevent **condensed water (water of condensation)** from dripping from the lid onto the agar surface, which would wash colonies together, cause spreading or confluent growth and risk contamination. Inverting keeps the surface dry so that discrete, well-separated colonies form.

> [!answer]
> So condensation on the lid does not drop onto the agar surface and spoil discrete colony growth.
hint: Think about condensation on the lid.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Plates are incubated **agar side up (lid down)**. A wet agar surface allows swarming organisms such as *Proteus* to spread and makes colony counting and picking impossible.

## Simplified explanation

Plates are turned upside down so **water does not drip** onto the agar.

body: Mention **two** uses of a **lawn culture**.
answer:
1. **Antimicrobial susceptibility testing** (Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion) — requires confluent, even growth.
2. **Bacteriophage typing** and phage work (plaque formation on a bacterial lawn).
3. Preparation of **bacterial suspensions/antigens or vaccines** in bulk.
4. Testing the action of disinfectants or of bacteriocins.

> [!answer]
> Antimicrobial susceptibility (disc diffusion) testing and bacteriophage typing; also bulk harvesting of growth.
hint: Even carpet of growth over the whole plate.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A lawn (carpet) culture is made by flooding or swabbing a standardised suspension (0.5 McFarland for disc diffusion) over the whole surface. Even inoculation is essential or zone diameters cannot be interpreted.

## Simplified explanation

A lawn is used for **drug sensitivity tests** and **phage typing**.

body: Differentiate between **selective media** and **differential media**.
answer:
| | Selective medium | Differential medium |
|---|---|---|
| Principle | Contains inhibitors that **suppress unwanted organisms** so that wanted ones grow | Contains indicators that make colonies of different organisms **look different** |
| Effect on growth | Some organisms do not grow | All organisms grow; they are distinguished by appearance |
| Examples | Thayer–Martin (gonococci), MacConkey (bile salts/crystal violet inhibit Gram-positives), Lowenstein–Jensen, mannitol salt (7.5% NaCl) | Blood agar (haemolysis patterns), MacConkey (lactose fermenters pink), TSI, EMB |

Some media, such as **MacConkey agar**, are both selective and differential.

> [!answer]
> Selective media inhibit unwanted organisms; differential media let organisms grow but make them look different.
hint: Stop growth versus show a difference.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Selective agents include antibiotics, dyes, bile salts, high salt and altered pH. Differential indicators include pH indicators with a fermentable sugar, blood (haemolysis) and H₂S indicators.

## Simplified explanation

**Selective** = only some can grow. **Differential** = all grow but look different.

body: How will you test whether a culture medium you have prepared is **sterile**?
answer:
Incubate a representative sample of the prepared batch (e.g. a few plates or tubes, usually 3–5% of the batch) **without inoculation** at 35–37°C for **24–48 hours** (some laboratories also incubate a set at room temperature) and examine for growth. **No growth** indicates the batch is sterile and fit for use; any growth means the batch is contaminated and must be discarded.

> [!answer]
> Incubate uninoculated plates/tubes from the batch overnight at 37°C — no growth means sterile.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

This **sterility check** is part of routine quality control of media, along with checks on pH, appearance, gel strength and **performance testing** with control organisms (growth of the target organism, inhibition of others, correct differential reactions).

## Simplified explanation

Incubate a few **unused** plates overnight; if nothing grows, the batch is sterile.

body: What is the difference between **blood agar** and **chocolate agar**?
answer:
| | Blood agar | Chocolate agar |
|---|---|---|
| Preparation | 5–10% sterile defibrinated blood added to molten base at about 45–50°C; red cells remain **intact** | Blood added to the base and **heated to about 70–80°C**, lysing the red cells (brown colour; no chocolate is used) |
| Nutrients released | Red cells intact, so X (haemin) and V (NAD) factors are not freely available | Lysis releases **haemin (X) and NAD (V)**, supporting fastidious organisms |
| Main use | General purpose and **differential** medium — shows α, β and γ **haemolysis** | Enriched medium for fastidious organisms — *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, *N. meningitidis* |
| Haemolysis | Can be read | Cannot be read (cells already lysed) |

> [!answer]
> Blood agar has intact red cells and shows haemolysis; chocolate agar is heated blood agar whose lysed cells release X and V factors for fastidious organisms, but it cannot show haemolysis.
hint: One is simply the other, heated.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Heating also inactivates NADases in the blood that would otherwise destroy V factor. Thayer–Martin medium is chocolate agar made selective with antibiotics (vancomycin, colistin, nystatin, trimethoprim).

## Simplified explanation

Chocolate agar is **blood agar that has been heated**, so the broken red cells feed fussy bacteria.

body: What are **two** possible errors that could have occurred if you find your subcultures had no growth after incubation for 48 hours?
answer:
Any two:

1. **Failure to inoculate properly** — the loop was not charged, or it was still hot and killed the inoculum.
2. **Non-viable or too small an inoculum** — the original culture was dead or too dilute.
3. **Wrong medium** — the organism is fastidious and the medium lacked the required growth factors, or the medium was inhibitory/selective against it.
4. **Wrong incubation conditions** — wrong temperature, or an anaerobe/capnophile incubated aerobically (no anaerobic jar or CO₂).
5. **Medium faulty** — not sterile, dried out, wrong pH, or contained residual antimicrobial/disinfectant.
6. Incubator failure, or plates not incubated at all.

> [!answer]
> e.g. the loop was too hot or no organism was picked up, or the organism needed conditions (anaerobic, CO₂, enriched medium) that were not provided.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A systematic approach to no-growth checks the three requirements for growth: a **viable inoculum**, a **suitable medium** and **suitable atmosphere/temperature**. Always include a positive control organism to show the batch of medium supports growth.

## Simplified explanation

Either nothing living was put on the plate, or the plate or the incubation conditions were wrong.

body: Explain why **flaming the inoculating instrument before and after each inoculation** is essential during subculturing.
answer:
**Before** inoculation: flaming sterilizes the loop (red heat destroys all organisms on it), so no organisms from a previous culture or from the environment are carried onto the fresh medium — this prevents **cross-contamination and false results**.

**After** inoculation: flaming destroys the organisms remaining on the loop before it is put down, protecting the worker and the laboratory from **contamination and infection** and preventing the spread of the organism to other cultures.

> [!answer]
> To sterilize the loop so no organisms are carried into the new culture (before) and none are carried out of it into the laboratory (after) — aseptic technique.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The loop must be heated to **red heat** along the wire and allowed to cool (or cooled on a sterile part of the agar) before touching the culture, otherwise the heat kills the inoculum. Flaming should be done carefully to avoid spattering infectious material.

## Simplified explanation

Flaming keeps the loop **clean going in and safe coming out**.
